title: From Al-Imran to At-Tawbah
intro: 40 days through surahs 3 to 9, from Al-Imran to At-Tawbah, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: This plan walks through surahs 3 to 9, beginning with Al-Imran, "The Family of Imran": 200 verses revealed in Medina. Imran is understood as the father of Maryam (Mary), whose story the surah tells. This prayer belongs to people firm in knowledge, described in the verse before. Its point is that guidance, once given, is still a gift to ask for: they pray not to lose it. "The Bestower" is al-Wahhab.

The Prophet Zakariyya (Zechariah), the guardian of Maryam (Mary), keeps finding food with her in the sanctuary, and she tells him it comes from Allah. Seeing this, the elderly prophet prays for a child of his own, though his wife is barren. Commentators draw out the point: he asked for what seemed impossible, trusting the One who hears prayer. The angels answer with news of a son, the Prophet Yahya (John).

Here the angels tell Maryam (Mary) that Allah has chosen her, purified her and honoured her above the women of creation. The point is her unique standing: Muslims revere her as one of the most honoured women who ever lived. She is the only woman the Quran mentions by name, and the 19th surah is named after her. The verses that follow announce the birth of her son, the Prophet Isa (Jesus).

The point is that real goodness costs something: the verse ties it to giving away what one truly loves, not only what is left over. Al-birr, translated here as "piety", means righteousness and goodness in the fullest sense. According to a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the companion Abu Talha responded by giving away his most prized orchard.

posts.display: And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate. And remember Allah's favour unto you: How ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts so that ye became as brothers by His grace.
posts.display_original: وَٱعْتَصِمُوا۟ بِحَبْلِ ٱللَّهِ جَمِيعًا وَلَا تَفَرَّقُوا۟ وَٱذْكُرُوا۟ نِعْمَتَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذْ كُنتُمْ أَعْدَآءً فَأَلَّفَ بَيْنَ قُلُوبِكُمْ فَأَصْبَحْتُم بِنِعْمَتِهِۦٓ إِخْوَٰنًا
posts.caption: The point is unity: believers are to hold together to "the cable of Allah" and not split apart, remembering that faith once turned enemies into brothers. Commentators link those former enemies with Aws and Khazraj, the two main Arab tribes of Medina, whose long feud ended when they embraced Islam. The "cable" is habl Allah, a rope, explained in several ways, including the Quran and Allah's covenant.

posts.display: Those who spend (of that which Allah hath given them) in ease and in adversity, those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind; Allah loveth the good.
posts.caption: The verse before describes a paradise as wide as the heavens and the earth. This one describes who it is prepared for: people who give in good times and bad, hold back their anger, and forgive. "The good" renders al-muhsinin, those who practise ihsan, excellence in doing good.

Near the end of Al-Imran, these verses describe "men of understanding" who remember Allah in every posture and reflect on the sky and the earth. The point is where that reflection leads: to the conviction that nothing was created in vain, and from there to prayer. According to a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once rose at night, looked up at the sky and recited this closing passage of the surah.

posts.display: O mankind! Be careful of your duty to your Lord Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate and from them twain hath spread abroad a multitude of men and women.
posts.display_original: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱتَّقُوا۟ رَبَّكُمُ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكُم مِّن نَّفْسٍ وَٰحِدَةٍ وَخَلَقَ مِنْهَا زَوْجَهَا وَبَثَّ مِنْهُمَا رِجَالًا كَثِيرًا وَنِسَآءً
posts.caption: An-Nisa, "The Women", is the fourth surah: 176 verses revealed in Medina, much of it on family, orphans and the rights of women. It opens by reminding all people that they come from a single soul. Commentators draw the point: humanity is one family, with duties to one another, and the verse goes on to name the ties of kinship. "Be careful of your duty" renders ittaqu, from taqwa.

This verse closes a section of family law with a gentle note: the rules are meant to lighten burdens, because people were created weak. Commentators have understood that weakness in various ways, from frailty in the face of desire to human limits in general.

Two duties are joined here: return whatever has been entrusted to you, and judge between people with justice. Amanat, "deposits" or trusts, covers anything placed in someone's care: property, responsibility, a secret. According to commentators such as Ibn Kathir, it was revealed when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ returned the keys of the Kaaba to their keeper, Uthman ibn Talha, but its command applies to everyone.

A verse about something everyday: the greeting. Muslims greet one another with as-salamu alaykum, "peace be upon you", and the verse calls for a reply at least as good, or better, such as adding "and the mercy of Allah". "Taketh count" means Allah keeps account of all things.

According to classical commentators, the passage around this verse concerns a theft in Medina and an attempt to pin it on an innocent man. Amid that, this verse holds the door open to anyone who has done wrong. Seeking forgiveness, istighfar, is a constant theme of the Quran.

A striking question: what would Allah gain by punishing anyone who is grateful and believes? Commentators explain the point: Allah has no need to punish, and gratitude and faith are what He asks. "Responsive" renders Shakir, literally "the Thankful" or "the Appreciative", One who recognises and rewards even small good. The verse comes right after a passage on hypocrisy that leaves the door to repentance open.

posts.display: But help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty. Help not one another unto sin and transgression.
posts.display_original: وَتَعَاوَنُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلْبِرِّ وَٱلتَّقْوَىٰ وَلَا تَعَاوَنُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلْإِثْمِ وَٱلْعُدْوَٰنِ
posts.caption: Al-Ma'idah, "The Table Spread", is the fifth surah: 120 verses from the Medinan period, and many scholars count it among the last surahs revealed. This line sets a rule for working with others: join in what is good and right, never in sin or aggression. It comes right after a warning not to let hatred of a people push anyone into wrongdoing. "Pious duty" renders taqwa.

The Quran tells the story of the two sons of Adam, known in tradition as Qabil and Habil (Cain and Abel). When one brother's offering is accepted, the other threatens to kill him. These are the words of the brother who refuses to raise his hand, even under threat. Commentators hold him up as a picture of restraint: his fear of Allah is stronger than any urge to strike back.

posts.display: Whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.
posts.display_original: مَن قَتَلَ نَفْسًۢا بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ أَوْ فَسَادٍ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًا وَمَنْ أَحْيَاهَا فَكَأَنَّمَآ أَحْيَا ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًا
posts.caption: One of the Quran's most quoted verses on the sanctity of human life: to kill one innocent person is like killing all humanity, and to save one life is like saving all. It follows the story of the two sons of Adam, and says this was decreed for the Children of Israel; a very similar teaching appears in the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law. Pickthall's "for other than manslaughter" means other than as lawful retribution for murder.

The surah's name comes from this story. The disciples of the Prophet Isa (Jesus) ask whether his Lord can send down a table spread with food from heaven, and he tells them to be mindful of Allah. Commentators read his reply as a gentle warning: believers should not test Allah with demands for signs. In the verses that follow, Isa prays for the table as a feast and a sign, and Allah promises to send it down.

In the surah's closing scene, set on the Day of Judgment, Allah declares what counts on that day: the truthfulness of the truthful. It follows an exchange in which the Prophet Isa (Jesus) answers Allah truthfully about what he had taught people. The reward is the Gardens and something more: Allah is pleased with them and they with Him, an image of contentment flowing both ways that returns in several other surahs.

posts.display_original: ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَجَعَلَ ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ وَٱلنُّورَ ثُمَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ بِرَبِّهِمْ يَعْدِلُونَ
posts.caption: Al-An'am, "The Cattle", is a Meccan surah of 165 verses, and its first verse sets out its theme. All praise belongs to the One who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light, yet some still set up rivals beside Him. The surah goes on to argue for Allah's oneness against the idol worship of Mecca. It is one of five surahs that open with "Praise be to Allah".

A lesser-known verse with a striking idea: every creature on land and every bird belongs to a community, umam, "peoples like unto you". Commentators explain that they too are created, provided for and known to Allah. "The Book" here refers to the record of His decrees.

posts.display: Not a leaf falleth but He knoweth it, not a grain amid the darkness of the earth, naught of wet or dry but (it is noted) in a clear record.
posts.display_original: وَمَا تَسْقُطُ مِن وَرَقَةٍ إِلَّا يَعْلَمُهَا وَلَا حَبَّةٍ فِى ظُلُمَٰتِ ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا رَطْبٍ وَلَا يَابِسٍ إِلَّا فِى كِتَٰبٍ مُّبِينٍ
posts.caption: The point is the completeness of Allah's knowledge: nothing is too small to escape it. The verse begins, before the part on screen, "And with Him are the keys of the Invisible. None but He knoweth them." Then it moves from the vast to the tiny: land and sea, a falling leaf, a single grain in the dark soil. "A clear record" is understood as the record of all things kept with Allah.

The Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) looks at a star, then the moon, then the sun, and rejects each as a lord because each one sets. Commentators differ on whether he was reasoning his own way to faith or leading his people to see the flaw in worshipping the heavens. Three verses later he turns to the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

posts.display: Revile not those unto whom they pray beside Allah lest they wrongfully revile Allah through ignorance.
posts.display_original: وَلَا تَسُبُّوا۟ ٱلَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ فَيَسُبُّوا۟ ٱللَّهَ عَدْوًۢا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ
posts.caption: The first sentence of this verse forbids insulting what others worship, lest they insult Allah in return out of ignorance. Scholars have drawn from it a wider principle: avoiding words that lead to greater harm. It was revealed in Mecca, when the Muslims were a small and persecuted community.

A generous arithmetic: a good deed brings a tenfold reward, while a bad deed counts only as one. A well-known hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari adds that a good deed merely intended is recorded too, and that rewards can be multiplied far beyond ten. The verse ends with a promise of fairness.

Near the close of Al-An'am, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told to declare that his whole life belongs to Allah: prayer, sacrifice, living and dying. Many Muslims recite this verse in the supplication that opens their prayer. "Sacrifice" renders nusuk, which can also mean acts of devotion in general.

Al-A'raf, "The Heights", is a Meccan surah of 206 verses. It retells the story of the Prophet Adam and his wife, and this is their prayer after eating from the forbidden tree. Commentators often contrast it with Iblis, who blamed Allah for his own straying: Adam and his wife instead own their wrong together and ask for forgiveness and mercy. Many Muslims know this short prayer by heart.

"O Children of Adam" is a call to all humanity. Clothing is presented as a gift that covers and adorns, and then the verse points beyond it: the best garment is libas at-taqwa, "the raiment of restraint from evil", meaning mindfulness of Allah. "Splendid vesture" means fine clothing.

The verse teaches a manner of prayer: call on Allah humbly and quietly, not with show or excess. Many commentators, Ibn Kathir among them, read "aggressors" here as those who overstep proper limits, including in how they pray. Al-A'raf takes its name from "the Heights", a place between the Garden and the Fire described a few verses earlier.

The Prophet Musa (Moses) returns from his meeting with Allah to find his people worshipping a calf. In his anger he seizes his brother, the Prophet Harun (Aaron), who explains that the people overpowered him. Musa's anger turns to prayer for them both. "Most Merciful of all who show mercy" is arham ar-rahimin.

The verse invites people to call on Allah by His names, and to leave those who distort them. "The fairest names" are al-asma al-husna, the Most Beautiful Names of Allah, such as the Merciful, the Forgiving and the Wise. A well-known hadith speaks of ninety-nine of them. Calling on Allah by His names is a central part of Muslim prayer and remembrance.

Near its end, Al-A'raf contrasts idols, which cannot even help themselves, with Allah. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told to declare where his own protection lies, and these are the words given to him. "Protecting Friend" renders wali, a guardian and close ally, and al-Wali is one of the names of Allah.

Three short instructions to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in one verse: hold to forgiveness, encourage what is good, and turn away from the ignorant. "Kindness" here renders al-urf, what is commonly recognised as good. Some classical scholars called it the most comprehensive verse in the Quran on good character.

posts.display: They only are the (true) believers whose hearts feel fear when Allah is mentioned, and when His revelations are recited unto them they increase their faith, and who trust in their Lord.
posts.caption: Al-Anfal, "The Spoils of War", is a Medinan surah of 75 verses, revealed after the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. It opens with a dispute over the spoils. Then it turns the believers to what truly defines them: hearts that tremble at the mention of Allah, faith that grows on hearing His verses, and trust in Him, tawakkul.

In a run of verses addressed to the believers, Al-Anfal names the things people hold dearest, wealth and children, and calls them a fitnah: a test or trial. Commentators explain that the test lies in how these blessings are handled. Almost the same words appear in At-Taghabun 64:15, which likewise points to the "immense reward" with Allah.

A principle the Quran states twice, here and in Ar-Ra'd 13:11: Allah does not change the blessing He has given a people until they change what is within themselves. In context it explains the fall of earlier nations, such as Pharaoh's people, who rejected the signs they were given.

At-Tawbah, "Repentance", has 129 verses from late in the Medinan period, and it is the only surah that does not open with the Bismillah. This verse answers those who were pleased when misfortune struck the believers. Its point is calm trust: nothing reaches the believers except what Allah has decreed for them, and He is their protector, so they rely on Him whatever comes.

The surah's name comes from tawbah, turning back to Allah in repentance, and this verse states its hope plainly: Allah accepts His servants' repentance and receives their charity. Commentators connect the passage with believers who had stayed behind from an expedition and then admitted their faults. "The Relenting" renders at-Tawwab, the One who accepts repentance again and again.

This follows the story of three companions who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk without excuse. One of them, Ka'b ibn Malik, chose to tell the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ the plain truth rather than invent excuses, and after fifty days their repentance was accepted. This verse draws the lesson: be with the truthful.

Near the end of At-Tawbah comes this portrait of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: one of the people themselves, grieved by their hardship, deeply concerned for them. "Full of pity, merciful" renders ra'uf and rahim, two words the Quran also uses of Allah.

The final verse of At-Tawbah: if people turn away, Allah is enough. Many Muslims repeat its words as part of their daily remembrance. That completes this journey through seven surahs, from Al-Imran to At-Tawbah. Thank you for reading along.
